opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the starting point was really a kind of puzzle. There was a lot of excitement around this idea that as you scale up language models, certain capabilities just suddenly appear. You'd look at these plots where performance is basically flat, near zero, across several orders of magnitude of model size, and then at some point it shoots up. And the story people were telling was that something qualitatively new was happening inside the model, almost like a phase transition.

What caught our attention, and Rylan Schaeffer, who was the lead student on this work, was really the one pushing on it, was that when you looked closely at which tasks showed this behavior, it wasn't uniform. It seemed to cluster around particular ways of measuring performance. A lot of the dramatic examples used metrics like exact match accuracy, where you only get credit if every single token in the output is correct. Or multiple choice grading that's all-or-nothing.

And if you think about that for a second, those metrics are inherently nonlinear, or discontinuous, in the underlying per-token quality of the model. Suppose the model's per-token accuracy is improving smoothly and predictably with scale, which is roughly what scaling laws tell us about things like cross-entropy loss. If you then require, say, ten tokens to all be right, your success probability goes like that per-token accuracy raised to the tenth power. That function stays near zero for a long time and then rises sharply. So you get something that looks like a sudden jump, even though nothing sudden is happening in the model itself.

So the question we asked was: is emergence a property of the model, or is it a property of how the researcher chose to measure the model? And that's a testable question. We could take the same model outputs and score them with a continuous or linear metric, like token edit distance or Brier score instead of accuracy, and see if the sharp transition goes away. In many cases it did. The performance curves became smooth and predictable.

We also flipped it around: could we induce apparent emergence in settings where nobody would claim it exists, like vision models, just by picking a harsh enough metric? And we could. That was a pretty strong signal that a lot of what was being called emergence was in the eye of the beholder, so to speak.

I want to be careful about the claim, though. We weren't saying models never gain new capabilities, or that nothing interesting happens with scale. The point was more that you should be skeptical of sharp transitions until you've checked whether they survive a change of metric, because that has real implications. If emergence is real and unpredictable, that's a big problem for safety and planning. If it's largely a measurement artifact, then capabilities may be much more forecastable than people feared, provided we measure the right things.

r001.rationale: The response says sharp transitions should be checked to see whether they survive a change of metric, framing metric sensitivity as evidence that the apparent emergence may be a measurement artifact. This communicates that fundamental emergence should be relatively robust to the metric used.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way this started was actually pretty mundane. We were looking at the emergence results that had gotten a lot of attention, where a model's ability on some task looks flat, basically at zero, across many scales, and then at some particular size it shoots up. And the claim that got attached to that was that these abilities are unpredictable, that they appear suddenly and discontinuously, and that you can't anticipate them from smaller models.

What caught our eye was that when you looked at which tasks showed emergence, it wasn't the tasks that seemed special. It was the metrics. Emergence showed up overwhelmingly on things like exact-match accuracy or multiple-choice accuracy, where you only get credit if every token in the answer is right. And it didn't show up, or showed up much less, on metrics that give partial credit, like token-level edit distance or log-likelihood of the correct answer.

That's a strange pattern if emergence is a fundamental property of the model. If the model really acquires a new capability at some scale, you'd expect to see that regardless of how you choose to score it. But if the sharp jump depends on which ruler you pick up, then the ruler is doing a lot of the work. And that's the thing that made it worth investigating rather than just an interesting anecdote.

The intuition is pretty simple once you see it. Suppose the model's per-token accuracy improves smoothly with scale. If your task requires getting, say, ten tokens in a row correct, then exact-match accuracy is roughly that per-token probability raised to the tenth power. A smooth, gradual improvement in the underlying quantity becomes an extremely sharp curve in the thing you're measuring. Nothing discontinuous is happening inside the model. The nonlinearity is in the metric. And then on top of that, you often have very few test samples at the small scales, so the low end of the curve gets resolved as zero when the true value is small but nonzero, which makes the jump look even cleaner.

So for us the metric dependence was both the clue and the hypothesis. It suggested a specific, testable alternative explanation: emergence is an artifact of discontinuous or nonlinear metrics applied to smoothly improving models, combined with insufficient resolution at small scales. And the nice thing is that's falsifiable. You can take the same model outputs, change the metric, and see whether emergence disappears. You can even go the other direction and induce apparent emergence in a setting like vision models, where nobody thought it existed, just by choosing the metric adversarially. That's the kind of thing you want from a scientific claim, and it's why the metric dependence felt like the right thread to pull.

r001.rationale: The response says a fundamental capability should appear regardless of how it is scored, so emergence depending on the chosen metric suggests the metric has substantial influence.

astra-6.text:
Well, the thing that stood out to us was that the claim seemed to depend on how you measured success. You could look at a model’s performance using one metric and see a sudden jump, but look at the same underlying predictions with another metric and see fairly smooth improvement. That raises a question: Is something changing abruptly in the model, or is the abruptness coming from the measurement?

For example, suppose you only count an answer as correct if the entire sequence is exactly right. The model might be steadily improving at predicting each individual token, but you don’t give it any credit until it gets everything right. That can make gradual progress look like a sudden appearance of a capability.

So we wanted to investigate how much of the reported emergence could be explained by that choice. It’s not that the improvements aren’t real. It’s that a sharp jump in a score doesn’t, by itself, establish a sharp change in the underlying capability. And that distinction matters if we want to understand and predict how models improve as we scale them.

r001.rationale: The response says metric choice can make improvement look abrupt or smooth, but does not state that a fundamental emergence phenomenon should be only weakly affected by the metric used.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the thing that stood out to us was that you could look at the same model outputs, change how you measured performance, and get a very different story about emergence. With one metric, it looks like nothing is happening and then suddenly the model acquires a capability. With another, you see fairly smooth improvement as you scale the model.

For example, if you only give credit when an entire answer is exactly correct, you can hide a lot of incremental progress. A model might be getting more and more of the answer right, but your metric keeps reporting zero until it crosses that threshold.

So that raised a question for us: how much of the apparent jump is a property of the model, and how much is a property of the measurement? It doesn’t mean that the capabilities aren’t real. It means we need to be careful about interpreting a sudden change in a score as evidence of a sudden change in the underlying capability.

r001.rationale: The response says measurement choice can change whether emergence looks sudden or gradual, but it does not state that a fundamental emergence phenomenon should be only weakly affected by the specific metric.
